{"commits":[{"authoredDate":"2026-09-16T02:57:20Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-16T02:57:20Z","messageBody":"_ios_scroll_to_element could spend seven minutes and 75 swipes and then
return None, logging nothing. #84 has been reproducible and
undiagnosable at the same time for exactly that reason: the failing case
is the one case with no record.

The sweep now records each step in memory and logs the whole trace at
the point it gives up. Silent on success by design -- a line per swipe
would drown the log for the case nobody is debugging -- and every exit
now carries a reason rather than a bare None.

The first trace it produced answers #84, and not the way the issue
guessed. Against row_60 with max_swipes=25:

      0.00s blind step 1/75 (down) swipe 629->262
      4.18s   fetch: target not in tree (unsettled read)
     ...
     15.07s   fetch: found and visible -- settling to confirm
     21.34s   confirm failed after settle -- target moved back out of view
     ...
    133.49s   fetch: found and visible -- settling to confirm
    138.62s   confirm failed after settle -- target moved back out of view
    413.31s GIVING UP: budget exhausted

The target was found, visible, twice. Both times the settle-and-confirm
correctly rejected it -- the fetch is unsettled, so it caught the row
mid-fling and the fling carried it out of view before the confirm ran.
What follows is the defect: a failed confirm is treated as never having
seen the target, and the sweep carries on in the same direction, away
from a row it had just located. It then exhausts 75 swipes and reports
not-found for an element it saw twice.

Also visible, and not the number the code assumes: describe_all costs
3.2-6.9s here against the ~1.8s cited in the comments, which is what
turns 75 swipes into 413 seconds.","messageHeadline":"Make the iOS scroll sweep say what it did when it fails","oid":"2fcdc4facd916afffc5121ec206bd40a4b548197"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-16T03:38:42Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-16T03:38:42Z","messageBody":"describe_all does two things: fetch the static tree, then hit-test every
container the walk reports as childless, to find hidden SwiftUI children
of tab bars and nav bars. The second is almost all of the cost, and
nothing said so -- the PERF line reported one total.

Measured on the 8-tab probe app, now that the line reports the split:

  total=3862.6ms (fetch=309.7ms probe=3552.9ms over 2 container(s))
  total=3742.5ms (fetch=163.9ms probe=3578.6ms over 2 container(s))

92% probe. It is structural rather than incidental: each container gets a
20-point horizontal hit-test sweep, and send() is serialised behind a
lock because the wire protocol carries no request IDs -- so the
asyncio.gather over those points reads as parallel and executes one at a
time. Forty round trips.

probe=False returns the static tree alone. Default stays True, so every
existing caller's answer is unchanged; this only gives a caller that
knows its target is in the static tree a way to say so. The flag is
carried through the poisoned-tree retry as well, or an opt-out would
silently pay again on recovery.","messageHeadline":"Let a caller skip container probing, and report what it costs","oid":"10471ffa5e6816bc488b034cb995dbc02a1900c5"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-16T04:21:21Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-16T04:21:21Z","messageBody":"The sweep's fetch runs once per swipe, up to 75 times, and each one was a
full describe_all -- including the container probe, which is 92% of the
call (fetch ~200ms against ~3.5s) and exists to find hidden children of
tab bars and nav bars.

The sweep is looking for a row in a recycling scroll container. Those are
always in the static tree; hidden tab-bar children are exactly what it
does not need. It paid ~3.5s per step for information it discarded.

Measured on tools/probe-app, row_60 from the top of a 200-row list with
max_swipes=25: a failing sweep went from 413s to 46.8s. It still failed
-- that is the next commit -- but it failed nine times faster.

Split out from the behaviour changes that follow so it can be kept or
dropped on its own: this one is pure cost, no semantics.","messageHeadline":"Stop the scroll sweep paying for container probing it cannot use","oid":"bb92d58d5a50775406a87a151eb71a603011c917"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-16T04:21:42Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-16T04:21:42Z","messageBody":"#84: scroll_to_element sweeps for minutes and reports not_found for an
element that is present. The trace showed the target found and visible
twice, and discarded both times.

Two causes, and the second only exists because of the first.

The search fetch was unsettled. wait_for_settle ran on the confirmation
path only, so the search read the tree mid-fling, caught the row in
flight, and the fling carried it out of view before the confirm re-read
-- which then correctly rejected a sighting that had been real when it
was taken. It now settles before the fetch, which the previous commit
made affordable.

And when a confirm does fail, the sweep now nudges back half a swipe and
re-checks rather than continuing away from the target. Previously `el`
reset to None and the loop treated a located row as never seen.

Verified on Xcode 27 / iOS 26.5 against tools/probe-app: row_60 from the
top of a 200-row list, max_swipes=25. Three runs failed before, three
passed after, 28s each.

This is the commit with field risk: it changes timing on every scroll in
every app, not just the failing case. Kept separate from the probe-skip
and the deadline so it can be backed out alone.","messageHeadline":"Settle before looking, and go back for a row the sweep already found","oid":"0caee1c61a722996047443e7d647522e56c7bed5"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-16T04:21:57Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-16T04:21:57Z","messageBody":"A swipe budget is not a time bound. The same 75 steps cost 25s or 500s
depending on what a tree read costs that day, and #84 produced sweeps of
413s and 523s against a caller that had given up at 180s.

Past a couple of minutes the answer is worthless regardless of whether it
is correct -- the screen it describes has moved on -- so continuing only
occupies a device something else is waiting for.

Independent of the two commits before it: this bounds the damage when a
sweep goes wrong for a reason nobody has found yet, rather than fixing
any particular one.","messageHeadline":"Bound the scroll sweep by wall-clock, not just by swipe count","oid":"f2268962540ee8af268f3fe5184b30567388ed06"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-16T03:38:54Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-16T04:21:57Z","messageBody":"Uvicorn does not cancel a handler when its client disconnects, so a
request the caller timed out of goes on working. Measured on #84: sweeps
of 413s and 523s continued against a client that left at 180s -- holding
a simulator the next test was trying to use, and swiping it while that
test ran. Back-to-back runs were not as independent as they looked.

scroll_to_element now runs as a task polled against is_disconnected(),
and is cancelled when nobody is listening. Polled rather than wrapped in
a timeout because there is no single right timeout here: how long the
operation should take is the operation's business, and it has its own
deadline now. This answers the narrower question of whether the answer
will be read by anyone.

Cancellation is cooperative, so the task stops at its next await and a
device command already in flight completes. That is the right side to err
on -- half-sending a command to the bridge is worse than finishing it.

The helper is deliberately general. Every long device operation has this
shape, and the others can adopt it once this one has proven itself.","messageHeadline":"Stop driving the device after the caller has gone","oid":"ec62abb0cf9551f8126e47ed75b5f813f77bd0bf"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-16T03:43:33Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-16T04:21:57Z","messageBody":"Both fixes landed without a test, and the settle broke three existing
ones on the way: the sweep now calls wait_for_settle, which the harness
had no stub for. Stubbing it is right -- the loop genuinely depends on it
now -- but the stub records rather than ignores, so the count can be
asserted.

The settle guard asserts one settle per swipe rather than merely that
settle was called. A single settle somewhere in the loop would satisfy
the weaker check while every other step still read the tree mid-fling,
which is the defect.

Mutation-tested both: replacing the settle with a literal
{"settled": True} fails the settle test and nothing else; the deadline
test fails if the check is removed.","messageHeadline":"Guard the settle and the deadline in the scroll sweep","oid":"d6d479803baaeb9ca905104b8624e357331a47b2"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-16T22:37:18Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-16T22:37:18Z","messageBody":"…es-no-trace","messageHeadline":"Merge remote-tracking branch 'origin/main' into fix/scroll-sweep-leav…","oid":"8e2e6939162bffa30414706ef70807f3c515e305"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-16T23:09:13Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-16T23:09:13Z","messageBody":"Review of #204 found `scroll_to_element` raising TypeError on three of
the four backends. `_native_ui_elements` passed `probe=False` when the
sweep asked to skip container probing, but only SimBridgeBackend accepted
the keyword. `_ui_backend` returns WdaBackend for physical iOS,
U2Backend for Android, and IdbBackend whenever sim-bridge is
unavailable -- which is the state a machine is in whenever SimulatorKit
cannot be found, as it could not for most of this week. The call raised
before fetching any UI at all.

Live testing missed it because every run went through sim-bridge, the one
backend that worked.

`probe` is now on all four signatures. Idb honours it, since it probes
the same way and pays the same ~3.5s. WDA and u2 accept and ignore it:
XCUITest's /source and uiautomator's dump both enumerate container
children, so there is nothing to probe and nothing to switch off. One
signature means the caller stops guessing which backend it has.

Four more from the same review:

The cold lookup probes again. A caller may ask to scroll to an element
only probing can see -- a tab-bar item is exactly that -- and skipping
the probe there hid the target from the one read that could have found it
without scrolling, sending the sweep to hunt something no swiping
reveals. Only the per-swipe lookups skip it, which is where the cost was.

The deadline covers the whole function rather than just the loop, so the
cold lookup and the screen-dimension reads fall inside it. Those are
cheap on a simulator and are not on a physical device, where one /source
read has been measured at 10.7s.

The reverse progress-check swipe settles before reading, for the reason
the search fetch does: a signature taken mid-fling describes a screen
still moving, and that one decides whether anything here scrolls at all.

_run_until_client_leaves has full type hints, and no longer converts its
own cancellation into a 499 -- that reported the caller as having
disconnected when it was the server shutting the request down.

Guarded by a signature check across all four backends, which fails if any
loses the keyword, and by a test that the cold lookup probes while the
sweep does not. Mutation-tested: removing it from idb alone fails both.

Re-verified: UI conformance 46 passed 0 failed on both platforms, unit
suite 2511.","messageHeadline":"Fix a crash the review caught: probe= reached backends without it","oid":"c67ea8f46267a81ab3ca07c4817c3552131f6cfd"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-16T23:34:18Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-16T23:34:18Z","messageBody":"The MCP tool description and the API reference both described the loop as
it behaved before this branch. An agent reading either would not predict
a settle between swipes, a first lookup that probes, a wall-clock bound,
or a 499.

The description is not decoration here: it is the only thing an agent
reads before choosing this tool and deciding what its failures mean. The
499 matters most of the three -- it is new on this endpoint, and an agent
that treats it as a transient error will retry a request nobody is
listening to. Named as non-retryable, with the reason.

Kept the claim about avoiding a full tree dump, which is still true of
the sweep, and qualified it for the cold lookup, which now deliberately
reads containers the static tree omits so a tab-bar item is found without
scrolling at all.

tsc clean; test_readme_sync passes, which is what checks the reference
against the routes and tools actually registered.","messageHeadline":"Say what the scroll loop now does, where agents will read it","oid":"89c28a797a676c46170105734257dfcbe488f6a2"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-16T23:52:17Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-16T23:52:17Z","messageBody":"Review of #204 found the 499 path unreachable when it matters most.
_send_locked catches CancelledError alongside TimeoutError -- correctly,
because the remedy is the same: the command was already written, the
protocol carries no request ids, and a late response would be handed to
whoever asks next, so the subprocess has to die either way.

Converting cancellation into a RuntimeError was the mistake. When
_run_until_client_leaves cancels the task because the client has gone,
that RuntimeError escaped instead of the cancellation, so the handler
never reached its 499 -- and the message claimed a timeout that had not
happened, which is the misreporting shape of #178 one layer down.

Cancellation is now re-raised, after the kill rather than before it. The
stale-response hazard is identical whichever way the wait ended, and a
cancellation that skipped the cleanup would leave exactly the
uncorrelated response the kill exists to prevent.

Swallowing CancelledError is worth avoiding on its own terms: it breaks
cancellation semantics for every caller, not only this one.

Guarded both ways -- cancellation propagates with the kill still
performed, and a timeout still becomes a RuntimeError. Mutation-tested:
removing the re-raise fails the first and leaves the second passing.","messageHeadline":"Let a cancelled sim-bridge command stay cancelled","oid":"d975074d9ff199be1957199ddbe0491208229eb3"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-17T00:38:53Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-17T00:38:53Z","messageBody":"The trace was emitted on the way out of a failure, which left the most
diagnosable case silent. Measured on iOS 18.6: the same scroll passed in
24s, 24s and 113s, and nothing in the log distinguished them. Working out
why the third was five times slower meant reconstructing it from
scattered [PERF] lines and a count of settle timeouts -- the same "failed
and there is no record" problem this branch set out to fix, surviving in
the case nobody thought to look at.

Every success now goes through one exit that logs the accumulated trace
when the sweep took longer than a quarter of its deadline. Silence on the
fast path stays the point: a line per scroll is noise, and noise is why
nothing was logged here in the first place.

The threshold is a fraction of the budget rather than a constant, so it
follows if the deadline is ever retuned instead of becoming a number
nobody revisits.

Guarded both ways -- a slow success logs, a fast one does not --
mutation-tested by suppressing the emit, which fails the first and leaves
the second passing. The slow test drives `perf_counter` rather than
racing it: a tiny real deadline trips the pre-lookup guard before
anything can be slow, and a large one needs a genuinely slow sweep, so
neither exercises the branch.

Verified on iOS 18.6 (iPhone 16 Plus): 25 passed. Unit suite 2517.","messageHeadline":"Trace a sweep that succeeds slowly, not only one that fails","oid":"52453ac63835881ca684c3bc7b76ebdbba1df249"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-17T04:49:54Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-17T04:49:54Z","messageBody":"Five of the review's findings. The disconnect guard itself is left for a
separate change -- see the last section.

A crashed bridge no longer looks cancelled. The previous commit made
_send_locked re-raise CancelledError so a disconnect-driven cancellation
would reach the caller. But CancelledError has a second source here:
_stdout_reader calls _cleanup_state() when the subprocess exits, which
cancels _pending_response. A bridge that died mid-command therefore
surfaced as a cancelled task, which skips every `except Exception`
fallback above this call. Task.cancelling() counts cancellation requests
against the current task, so it separates the two exactly: re-raise only
when this task was cancelled, otherwise report a failed command. The
tests now drive both sources for real -- cancelling the task, and
cancelling the future the way the reader does -- where the old test
patched wait_for and could not tell them apart.

tap_element is guarded too. With scroll_to_find on, which is the default,
an off-screen target runs the same sweep, and that is the path most
callers reach it by. Guarding only scroll_to_element covered the rare
entry point and left the common one unbounded.

A probe-only target no longer sets off a blind sweep. The sweep skips
probing to save its cost, which is only sound for a target the static
tree can see. A tab-bar item located by the cold lookup but not on
screen was lost at the first plain read and hunted blindly -- 30 swipes
and 31 reads in the review's scenario, where main gave up after 2. One
plain read now decides: if it cannot see the target, the sweep keeps
probing, the target stays located, and the existing stall check ends it
after two swipes, because chrome does not scroll. Back to 2.

Two comments corrected. The deadline does not cover the screen-dimension
reads, which run before it; one said it did. And one nudge per sighting
does let the sweep oscillate -- bounded by the swipe budget and the
deadline, but the comment claimed it could not.

The 499 is no longer advertised. The guard cannot fire in production:
APIKeyMiddleware is a Starlette BaseHTTPMiddleware, and through it
request.is_disconnected() never reports a disconnect. The review
isolated it by running the guard behind each middleware in turn -- it
works behind none, CORS, and Timeline, and fails behind the auth
middleware alone. The guard's logic is correct and stays; the fix is to
the middleware, and belongs in its own change rather than a scroll one.
The docs and MCP description stop promising a status nothing can
return, and the deadline wording now says iOS, since Android has none.

Unit suite 2518. Two existing scroll tests gained a read: their scripted
UI responses now include the plain read that decides probe-only-ness.","messageHeadline":"Act on the second review: a crash read as a cancel, and more","oid":"6b75c370c3a7d9ea3a42a1235f0cd022e4290596"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-17T05:20:56Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-17T05:20:56Z","messageBody":"A review of #204 mutation-tested the sweep and found ten of eleven
changes to it survived the suite. The worst: moving the settle to after
the search read passed, because the test named for it compared the
number of settles to the number of swipes, which settling afterwards
satisfies just as well. The #84 fix was unguarded. So was the nudge-back,
which had no test at all.

Most of what survived is about order -- settle before looking, which way
to go back -- and the existing harness, which moves the screen by a
fixed offset, cannot express order. The new one records every swipe,
settle, read and hit-test in sequence, serves scripted reads, and has its
clock advanced by hand rather than raced. Each test names the mutant it
exists to kill.

Result, against a clean copy of this tree:

    before (review)   1 of 11 killed
    now              15 of 15 killed

Each is killed by exactly one test, which is the useful shape: a test
precise about what it protects, not one that happens to catch several.

The fifteen include four this branch added since the review -- a crash
re-raised as a cancellation, a real cancellation swallowed, the
probe-only check removed, and tap_element left unguarded. The last
started life as a mutant whose replacement was identical to its
original, which would have "survived" forever while testing nothing; it
was replaced with a genuine unwrap before the run.

Covered now: settle-before-read ordering; the swipe back after a lost
sighting, and its direction, and that it settles before reading; the
slow-success trace on the confirm and reverse paths, not only the cold
one; the deadline stopping a sweep mid-run rather than only before the
first read; the reverse branch settling before its hit-test; a
probe-only target keeping the sweep probing; `probe=False` surviving the
poisoned-tree retry and being honoured by idb, not merely accepted; the
disconnect guard cancelling work and returning 499; and tap_element
running under that guard.

The disconnect tests carry a caveat in their module docstring: the guard
does not fire in production until #208, because the auth middleware
defeats is_disconnected(). They test that the guard is correct, not that
disconnects are handled end to end.

Unit suite 2532.","messageHeadline":"Guard the sweep's behaviour, not just its call counts","oid":"bf2f054246812ce69eecd6fa33c1c21b12a322ba"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-17T05:22:32Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-17T05:22:32Z","messageBody":"…es-no-trace","messageHeadline":"Merge remote-tracking branch 'origin/main' into fix/scroll-sweep-leav…","oid":"23deade8578def8ddcaaea7a7209e60294d16795"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-17T07:06:20Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-17T07:06:20Z","messageBody":"The slow-success trace answered #84 in one run. On iOS 18.6 a 0.3s sweep
swipe flung the list 1020pt for a 389pt drag -- more than a screen -- so
row 20 landed under the nav bar after one swipe and left the tree after
the next. The sweep then lost its direction and restarted downward: 32
swipes, 105.8s. Every between-swipe settle timed out, because the
flings outlasted it.

Swipes. sim-bridge's swipe takes a `hold`: the finger stays down at the
end point before lifting. Repeating the identical point changed nothing
(still ~1000pt), so the hold alternates by half a thousandth of the
screen; with that, travel is the drag (350pt) and the list is at rest on
release. Sweep swipes are held and cover 75% of the screen, 625pt
measured, which is less than the visible area, so no row can be passed
over. WDA's drag was already controlled: 358pt drag, 349pt travel,
nothing moving after the call returned, including at the end of a list.
idb cannot hold and says so (`swipe_is_controlled = False`), and keeps a
settle per step.

Reads. The per-step settle is gone. A read is repeated until two agree,
because a drag past the end of a list snaps back on release -- measured
91pt off on the fixture list -- and ~50ms reads are far cheaper than a
~1.5s screenshot settle. WDA returns once the app is idle
(`swipe_returns_at_rest = True`), so there each read is taken once. With
every read at rest a sighting is final, and the confirm-and-nudge-back
logic has nothing left to do.

Ends. Whether a swipe moved anything is read from the same full-tree
read that looks for the target, by fingerprint (identity and position).
An unchanged tree going down turns the sweep around; going up, it ends
the search. This replaces the hit-test progress check, which ran once
and on a physical device cost six full /source reads (~25s) -- WDA has
no hit-test -- while the sweep still spent its downward budget at the
bottom of a list whose target was above: 94s for Wi-Fi from the bottom
of Settings on an iPhone 11.

That check was also wrong on iOS 26. WDA's emulated hit-test took the
last element containing the point, and Settings has full-screen `Other`
views after its rows, so every point resolved to an overlay that never
moves: 3 of 4 Settings targets reported not found. It now takes the
smallest containing element. This is on main too, since f962b18.

Budget. Down for up to 2x max_swipes, 3x in all as before: a controlled
swipe travels less than a flung one, and an even split no longer reached
row 199 of 200 at the default budget. A lost target keeps the direction
it was in.

Measured, before -> after:

  iPhone 16 Plus sim, iOS 18.6
    conformance scroll test        105s -> 19s
    whole conformance suite        436s -> 300s (same 105 pass)
    row_199 from the top           404 at 28s -> found at 15.5s
  iPhone 11, iOS 26.6.2, Settings
    Wi-Fi from the bottom          94s -> 24s
    Developer / General / Privacy  34s / 36s / 27s -> 20s / 19s / 14s

Tests: test_scroll_sweep_behaviour.py is rebuilt around a modelled lazy
list (rows, clamped ends, bounce, idb and WDA variants), and every test
names the mutant it kills. 26 mutants, all killed.","messageHeadline":"Rebuild the iOS sweep on controlled swipes and at-rest reads","oid":"a58af93d2f9df19a18d90eefdb74d17255619e04"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-17T14:32:50Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-17T14:32:50Z","messageBody":"…rows

A review from a separate session (dev-34, PR comment 5715526846) found two
real problems and a set of smaller ones, all verified against the model
before fixing. It also found that the model hid the first one.

idb still flings, and its step was the controlled backends' 75%. With a
2.6x fling that passes over 87 of 200 rows from the top. The model moved
the list by exactly the drag even for idb, so every test stayed green.
idb now drags a quarter of the screen. The model now follows measurement:
controlled travel is 0.9x the drag, an unheld swipe 2.6x, and a bounce
decays over three reads rather than one.

A label that changes in place, such as a clock or a progress percentage,

full 2.5s after the last check is time spent past what the caller was
promised. The settle is the one step inside an iteration that takes a
timeout, so it is now given what is left of the deadline, and skipped
when that is nothing. Threading the remaining time through the reads
themselves is the rest of that finding and is filed separately.
